name: Battle of Adwa
info: On 1 March 1896 an Ethiopian army under Emperor Menelik II defeated an Italian colonial force under General Oreste Baratieri near Adwa, ending the First Italo-Ethiopian War and leading Italy to recognise Ethiopian sovereignty in the Treaty of Addis Ababa.

facts.place: Near the town of Adwa, in the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, on the mountains and in the valleys west and south of the town
facts.sides: The Ethiopian Empire under Emperor Menelik II, with estimates of between 73,000 and over 100,000 men; an Italian colonial force under General Oreste Baratieri, estimated at 14,519 effective combat troops by Harold Marcus and at 17,770 with fifty-six artillery pieces by David Levering Lewis
facts.outcome: An Ethiopian victory: over 6,000 Italian and colonial troops were killed and around 3,800 captured, by one set of figures. Italy later signed the Treaty of Addis Ababa, recognising Ethiopia as independent.

t: The war began from a dispute over Article 17 of the Treaty of Wuchale, which the Italian text read as making Ethiopia a protectorate of Italy and the Amharic text read as an offer of Italy's good offices.
Baratieri attacked under pressure from Rome and from his own generals, and his columns, advancing on poor maps, lost touch with one another and were defeated one after another.
Prisoners were treated unequally: about 800 captured Eritrean askari were mutilated, and around 70 Italian prisoners were massacred in retaliation for the death of Bashah Aboye.
dyk: The Italian army at Adwa consisted mainly of white European troops, unlike most European armies of the Scramble for Africa, and the newer Carcano Model 91 rifles were not issued according to Chris Prouty, because Baratieri was under constraints to be economical and wanted to use up the old cartridges.
ev: Italy and King Menelik of Shewa sign the Treaty of Wuchale, whose Italian and Amharic versions of Article 17 differ
Baratieri defeats Ras Mengesha Yohannes at Coatit in January, and Menelik issues a call to arms to the whole population in September
An Ethiopian vanguard destroys a small Italian unit at Amba Alagi on 7 December, and the Italians withdraw to more defensible positions in Tigray
On 29 February Baratieri meets his generals, who argue for an attack rather than a retreat
The Italian columns advance after midnight and the battle is fought on 1 March, ending in the collapse of all four brigades
Baratieri reaches Adi Keyh on 2 March and telegraphs news of the defeat to Rome
Prime Minister Crispi resigns on 9 March, and Italy later signs the Treaty of Addis Ababa
Italy launches the Second Italo-Ethiopian War on 3 October, and Ethiopian forces are defeated by May 1936

sections.background:
In 1889 Italy signed the Treaty of Wuchale with King Menelik of Shewa. It recognised Italy's claim to the coastal colony of Eritrea. A dispute arose over Article 17. In the Italian version the Emperor of Ethiopia was obliged to conduct all foreign affairs through Italian authorities, which would make Ethiopia a protectorate. The Amharic version said he could use Italy's good offices if he wished. Italian diplomats claimed that the Amharic original held the clause and that Menelik knowingly signed a modified copy.

Between 1890 and 1896 Italy pursued two strategies. One, nicknamed "politica scioana", was diplomatic: persuading Menelik to accept the Italian reading and enlisting other European powers. The other, "politica tigrigna", relied on the Ministry of Colonies and the government of Eritrea and exploited the resentment of Tigray against the new Shewan emperor, in the hope of dismembering the country. Menelik resisted both, and in June 1894 the leading figures of Tigray travelled to Addis Ababa to pay homage to him. Italy then chose a military solution. Baratieri defeated Ras Mengesha at Coatit in January 1895 and by late 1895 had occupied much of Tigray.

Menelik issued a call to arms in September 1895, and on 7 December his vanguard destroyed a small Italian unit at Amba Alagi. By late February 1896 supplies on both sides were running low. Baratieri knew the Ethiopians were living off the land, and that once the peasants' stores were exhausted their army would begin to melt away, but the Italian government insisted that he act.
sections.forces:
Estimates for the Ethiopian army under Menelik range from 73,000 to over 100,000 men, which outnumbered the Italians about five times. The regional forces were listed by their rifles: 25,000 from Shewa under Menelik, 3,000 under Empress Taytu, 5,000 from Gojjam under Negus Tekle Haymanot, 15,000 from Harar under Ras Makonnen, 12,000 from Tigray under Ras Mengesha Yohannes and Ras Alula, 6,000 from Wollo under Ras Mikael, 8,000 from Gondar and 6,000 from Lasta, with about 20,000 spearmen and swordsmen besides. The armies were followed by a similar number of camp followers. Menelik's aim was to preserve Ethiopian independence, and Italy's was to make Ethiopia accept the Italian text of the treaty.

Immediately before the battle the Italian army in East Africa numbered around 29,700, but several thousand were needed to guard the lines of communication. Marcus estimates 14,519 effective combat troops at Adwa. Lewis estimates four brigades totalling 17,770 troops with fifty-six artillery pieces. They were led by Baratieri, with Albertone's native brigade on the left, Arimondi in the centre, Dabormida on the right and Ellena in reserve. Many of the troops were inexperienced conscripts drafted into new battalions. The historian Chris Prouty lists inadequate maps, old-model guns, poor communication equipment, inferior footgear, low morale and a shortage of mules and saddles. After a meeting on the evening of 29 February at which Baratieri proposed retreat and his brigadiers argued for an attack, he announced the advance.
sections.course:
The Italian columns marched after midnight to take three heights in parallel, with Albertone setting the pace. Albertone went astray, apparently misled by a map based on local accounts, and was led as far as Mount Abba Gerima, cut off from the rest. An informant working as Baratieri's interpreter, Awalom of Enticho, reported the movements to Ras Alula, and the commanders of the imperial army joined the battle. Menelik was at prayer in the church of St George and was not present at the start.

Around 6:00 a.m. Albertone's vanguard was charged by Ethiopian units, and two mountain batteries were captured with their commanders killed. His askaris held for over two hours. Menelik, shaken, considered retreat, but Empress Taytu and Ras Mangasha persuaded him to release his reserve of 25,000. At 8:30 a.m. Albertone's brigade began a retreat that became a rout, and Albertone was captured. Dabormida's brigade, drawn into the valley of Mariam Shewito, was cut off by Ras Makonnen, with a gap of about two miles.

The Ethiopians then attacked Arimondi's brigade. It was outflanked on the right and the left, and gave way at around 12:00. Baratieri ordered a general retreat, which was poorly coordinated, and Ras Mikael's Oromo cavalry cut down fleeing men. Colonel Galliano's battalion collapsed, and by eyewitness accounts he was captured and executed. A rearguard of barely one hundred Alpini was annihilated. Dabormida's last assault, with the cry "Forward, Savoy!", was repulsed, and he disappeared in the final stage.
sections.aftermath:
Casualty figures differ. George Berkeley records 6,133 Italian and colonial dead, 1,428 wounded and 1,865 Italians and 2,000 askari taken prisoner, with Ethiopian losses of 7,000 killed and 10,000 wounded. Richard Caulk estimates 5,900 dead, 1,000 wounded who escaped and at least 2,000 captured, with Ethiopian losses of 3,886 killed and 6,000 wounded. The Italians left behind all their artillery, 11,000 rifles and most of their transport. Menelik did not pursue them into Eritrea, though Ras Alula favoured it.

About 800 captured Eritrean askari, regarded by the Ethiopians as traitors, had their right hands and left feet amputated. Augustus Wylde, who visited the field months later, reported a pile of severed hands and feet still visible and the neighbourhood of Adwa full of the freshly dead, many of whom had crawled to streams and lingered unattended until they died. Italian prisoners were generally treated better, though with some abuse, possibly including castration. General Albertone was given a tent, a horse and servants. Around 70 Italian prisoners were massacred in retaliation for the death of Bashah Aboye, and the officer responsible was reportedly imprisoned by Menelik.

News of the defeat provoked street demonstrations in many Italian cities. Prime Minister Francesco Crispi resigned on 9 March, and King Umberto declared his birthday on 14 March a day of mourning. Menelik limited his demands to little more than the abrogation of the Treaty of Wuchale.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from later historians and a few contemporary witnesses. The historians include George Berkeley, whose study of the campaign was first published in 1902, Richard Caulk, Harold Marcus, David Levering Lewis, Chris Prouty, Paul Henze and Richard Pankhurst. Among the witnesses are Alexander Bulatovich, who wrote an account of an expedition with Menelik's armies, and the Italian reporter Adolfo Rossi, who warned of an overstretched army and was expelled from the colony days before the defeat. Eyewitness accounts supply details such as Galliano's execution, and Augustus Wylde visited the field.

Several points are disputed or uncertain. The strengths of both armies are estimates: 73,000 to over 100,000 for the Ethiopians, and 14,519 against 17,770 for the Italians. Berkeley's and Caulk's casualty figures differ, and Caulk cites contemporary figures for the Ethiopian losses. The cause of Albertone's wrong turn is described only as likely confusion arising from the map. The circumstances of Dabormida's death remain unclear, and his last message to Baratieri never arrived. Historians also differ on why Menelik did not pursue. Prouty notes that a failure of nerve has been alleged by Italian and Ethiopian sources, Lewis suggests Menelik feared that destroying Baratieri would turn a colonial war into a national crusade, and Marcus points to a restive army, short rations and the coming rains. Carlo Conti Rossini argued that two more weeks of war would have ended in Ethiopian defeat.
sections.legacy:
As a direct result of the battle Italy signed the Treaty of Addis Ababa, recognising Ethiopia as an independent state. Paul Henze calls the battle a fundamental turning point in Ethiopian history, and Bahru Zewde observes that few events in the modern period have brought Ethiopia so much to the world's attention. The defeat of a colonial power became a rallying point for later African nationalists and Pan-Africanists. Richard Pankhurst writes that the victory gave Ethiopians immense pride and made the country, in the eyes of many Africans, a beacon of independence in a continent almost entirely enslaved by colonialism. Donald Levine adds that it encouraged isolationist and conservative strains in Ethiopian culture.

In Italy it was a humiliation. Tripodi argued that some of the roots of Fascism went back to this defeat and the wish to avenge it, and Mussolini declared in May 1936 that Adwa had been avenged. The Second Italo-Ethiopian War began on 3 October 1935, with tanks, aircraft and chemical warfare, and Ethiopian forces were defeated by May 1936. Italy occupied Ethiopia for five years before British Empire forces and Ethiopian guerrillas drove it out.

Adwa Victory Day is a public holiday across Ethiopia, marked at Menelik Square in Addis Ababa and in Adwa itself. The commemorations honour Empress Taytu and recall that thousands of women took part in the battle as nurses and in supplying food and water.

summary: The Battle of Adwa, fought on 1 March 1896, was the climax of the First Italo-Ethiopian War. Emperor Menelik II's army defeated General Baratieri's Italian force, and Italy recognised Ethiopian independence in the Treaty of Addis Ababa.

notes: The article gives the Italian march as around 9 p.m. on the 27th, but the Background gives the meeting on the evening of 29 February and the march after midnight. I followed the Background and wrote only after midnight on 1 March. Please check against a second source.
The article says the 3,800 captured (lead) while Berkeley gives 1,865 Italians and 2,000 askari and Caulk at least 2,000. Facts line says by one set of figures.
The article uses spellings Eritrean Ascari and askari; I used askari.
The Italian side's aims are given only in the Background (force acceptance of the Italian text, protectorate); I did not add more.
Order-of-battle detail (rifles per column, battalions) was left out for length.

The sources section rests mostly on the article's citation of historians; it names few contemporary eyewitnesses. Bulatovich and Rossi are named from the Sources list and Background; I did not say what Bulatovich wrote about the battle itself.
